newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kinkel sees progress, not breakthrough, at summit.
newsitem.headline: Kinkel sees progress, not breakthrough, at summit.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said on Wednesday he expected substantial progress but no breakthrough on NATO enlargement at a summit between Boris Yeltsin and Bill Clinton starting on Thursday.

"I don't expect a breakthrough in the sense that Russia says 'Yes, we approve of NATO enlargement', or concrete results on a G8 (including Russia in the Group of Seven industrial powers)," Kinkel told German Radio.
But he added there would "certainly be concrete results".

Kinkel said Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov had made "not insubstantial" progress in his talks in Washington to prepare for the summit, and had promised to call his German counterpart after the summit to discuss the outcome.
"These are all steps that can and should be finalised (at a NATO summit) in July. I am convinced, without wanting to raise unjustified hopes, that we can and will be successful," he said.

Kinkel also said there had been substantial progress in the negotiations which NATO is holding with Moscow to give Russia a firmly defined place in the new, post-Cold War European security architecture.

"As far as the NATO-Russia charter is concerned, we have already started working on the text and have already got much further than is generally known," he said, adding that he believed Russia could at least be convinced the West was serious about including it in European security planning.
He said the two sides would set up a "NATO-Russia Council", in which Russia had an equal voice, and which would take all decisions which affected both NATO and Russia.
Progress was being made on the thorny question of limits for the troops and conventional weapons NATO could station on the territory of its new members.
"NATO has set certain upper limits, but the Russians have not agreed yet," Kinkel said.

He added that Moscow would also have influence on NATO by means of its permanent membership of the United Nations Security Council, which will be asked to approve any NATO decisions affecting areas outside its own territory.

Kinkel said that, as part of the NATO-Russia talks, Moscow had presented NATO with four papers dealing respectively with bilateral cooperation, NATO's transformation, joint consultation and decision-making mechanisms, and lastly with military-political issues.

"That one contains the most difficult questions," he said. "That deals with the problem of whether soldiers will be stationed in the new territories, what will be done about infrastructure, former Russian airbases and so on...
"NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana has set against that an alliance draft for a security charter which includes the issues I have just mentioned."
